title: Provision servers with Terraform
description: Describe cloud servers as Terraform files, read what kikx writes, and see how those servers reach your inventory.
outcomes: Know when to provision and when to skip it
Pick a provider and fill region, size, image and count
Read the generated .tf file line by line
Connect provisioned servers to an inventory and see them in Architecture

steps.intro: This lesson is about the very first stage of a project: creating the machines themselves. I'll drive, and you'll take over twice.
steps.why: Terraform creates servers at a cloud provider; Ansible then configures them. Machines have to exist before anything can be installed on them, so Provision comes first. If your servers already exist, you simply skip this stage.
steps.name: We start with a fresh project.
steps.optional: The start panel lists the stages in order. Provision is marked optional for exactly the reason above: nothing else depends on kikx creating the servers.
steps.serverName: The name matters more than it looks. It becomes the Terraform resource name, the file name, and the prefix of every machine Terraform creates.
steps.provider: Next, the provider: where the server will live.
steps.providerList: This list is not hard coded. It is every Terraform item in the kikx registry, so a new provider in the registry shows up here without a new release.
steps.providerFields: Each provider asks for its own fields. Switching provider resets them, because one provider's values rarely make sense at another.
steps.region: The region is the data centre the server runs in. Pick one close to your users for lower latency, or one in a given country when data has to stay there. The placeholder shows a value this provider accepts.
steps.size: The size is the machine type: how many CPUs and how much memory you pay for. Names differ per provider, and you can resize later by changing this one value.
steps.image: The OS image is the system installed on first boot. The list is only a shortcut: any image this provider accepts works.
steps.count: Count is how many identical machines to create from this one description. One is fine for now.
steps.preview: Here is the file kikx renders, live, as you type. It is plain Terraform you can read, review and commit.
steps.token: The API token is declared as a sensitive variable and never written into the file. You pass it at apply time through an environment variable or a gitignored tfvars file.
steps.resource: This is the server itself: one resource, named after the component.
steps.names: Each machine gets the component name plus its index, starting at zero, so this server becomes web-0. Remember that name: it is how the inventory finds it.
steps.location: And here is the region you typed. Each provider names it its own way, kikx maps the field for you.
steps.add: Add the server to the project.
steps.secondWhy: Real projects rarely have one machine. A database usually lives apart from the web servers, and nothing stops you from using a different provider for it: each file carries its own provider block and its own token.
steps.secondTask: Your turn: add a second cloud server named db at DigitalOcean, give it a region and a size, then add it. Stuck? Press Show me.
steps.rows: Both servers are now in the project, each in its own .tf file. Terraform reads every file in the folder together, so one apply creates them all.
steps.handover: Terraform creates the machines, but Ansible needs to know where they are. kikx does not read Terraform state: after apply, Terraform tells you each server's address, and you list it in an inventory.
steps.addresses: Name each host the way Terraform does, web-0, web-1 and so on, and put them in a group named after the server. kikx uses those names to link the two.
steps.inventoryTask: Your turn: add an inventory named hosts, with one host web-0 at 203.0.113.10 in the group web, then add it to the project.
steps.diagram: Now open Architecture to see how kikx connects the pieces.
steps.serverNode: Provisioned servers sit in the Provision lane, with their region and size underneath.
steps.edge: This arrow says the web server provisions the web group. kikx draws it because the group shares the server's name and its host, web-0, follows Terraform's naming.
steps.groupNode: Here is the group from your inventory, in the Inventory lane, with its host count.
steps.fallback: The db server has no group of its own yet, so kikx links it to the top level groups. Add a db group to the inventory and the arrow becomes precise.
steps.done: You now know the whole provisioning loop: describe servers, read the Terraform, apply it, then list the machines in an inventory so Ansible can configure them.

checks.secondAdded: A server named db is in the project
checks.inventoryAdded: An inventory named hosts is in the project

recap: Provision is optional: skip it when your servers already exist.
Providers come from the registry; each asks for its own region, size and image.
Tokens stay out of the file as sensitive variables you pass at apply time.
Machines are named after the server plus an index, which is how kikx links them to inventory groups.
Architecture shows each server in the Provision lane and draws what it provisions.
